teaser: A royal family portrait built like an argument, with one empty cradle at its center.
review_notes:
Fee of 18,000 livres: widely cited, please confirm.
The gallery glimpsed at left is usually identified as the Hall of Mirrors (the scene being set in the Salon de la Paix).
Salon of 1787 anecdote: frame left empty for the first days and the quip 'Voilà le déficit' come from period accounts, worth checking the wording.
Sophie originally painted in the cradle then painted out: common account, not proven by published technical study as far as I know.
Jacques-Louis David advising a Raphael-style pyramid comes from Vigée Le Brun's circle/memoirs.
Queen had the painting removed after the Dauphin's death in June 1789: from Vigée Le Brun's memoirs.

lesson.text: This canvas was made for one building: the Palace of Versailles. It was meant to hang in the state rooms, where crowds of visitors walked through every day. The palace is even inside the picture. On the left edge, a row of tall arched openings is usually read as the Hall of Mirrors. The queen of France is sitting at home, and home is the center of power.

It was ordered in 1785 by the king's office of buildings, and it had a job to do. Marie Antoinette was hated. Pamphlets called her a spendthrift foreigner. A portrait of her in a simple cotton dress had shocked people in 1783, and a swindle over a diamond necklace, in which she was in fact innocent, had ruined what was left of her name.
Élisabeth Vigée Le Brun is said to have been paid 18,000 livres for this painting, more than the crown usually paid for the grandest history paintings of the time.

So nothing here is casual. The canvas is about 2.75 meters tall (9 feet), the size reserved for kings. Each child, each prop, even the queen's bare neck, answers an accusation. Go through them one by one.

lesson.title: The case for the queen
lesson.text: Four answers to her critics, each one painted with great care.

spots.title: A queen without a necklace
spots.text: Her face is calm, a little distant. She wears pearl earrings, but her neck is bare. After the necklace scandal, leaving diamonds out was a statement.

spots.title: Marie-Thérèse
spots.text: The eldest, about eight, hugs her mother's arm and looks up at her. Her gaze tells you where to look, and how to feel about this woman.

spots.title: Louis Charles
spots.text: The toddler squirms on her lap as real two-year-olds do. He is the future Louis XVII, a king who would never reign.

spots.title: The jewel cabinet
spots.text: A huge cabinet for the queen's jewels stands in the shadows, closed and pushed to the back. Its place in the picture is the whole point.

lesson.text: Educated viewers got the hint at once. In an old Roman story, a noblewoman named Cornelia was asked to show her jewels. She pointed to her sons and said that these were her jewels. The painter puts the real jewels in the dark and the children in the light.
A state portrait is not a snapshot. It is a message, and here the message is: this queen is a mother first.

How do you make a family look steady and almost sacred? Vigée Le Brun is said to have asked the painter Jacques-Louis David for advice. The answer was to borrow from Raphael's Holy Families, Renaissance pictures in which Mary and the children form a pyramid.
Three lines hold this big canvas together.

lines.label: The pyramid
lines.text: From the feathers of the hat down to the spread of red velvet, mother, daughter and baby fit inside one triangle. It is the shape of a Renaissance Madonna.

lines.label: The daughter's gaze
lines.text: The girl looks up at her mother's face. One short line of affection, aimed at the spot the painter wants you to end on.

lines.label: The pointing hand
lines.text: The older boy stands outside the pyramid. One hand lifts the cover, the other points. His arm drags your eye away from the group, toward something else.

lesson.text: That boy is Louis Joseph, the Dauphin, which was the title of the heir to the French throne. He is not looking at his mother or at his brother. He is showing you something.
What is the Dauphin pointing at? Tap the place where someone is missing.

spots.title: The empty cradle
spots.text: Under the dark green cover, the cradle holds only white sheets. The queen's fourth child, Sophie, died in June 1787, not yet one year old, while the painting was being finished.

lesson.text: Sophie is generally thought to have been painted in the cradle at first, then removed after her death. What stayed is a gap in the middle of a picture designed to show a full, happy family. The propaganda suddenly carries real grief.

At the Salon of 1787, the big public art show in Paris, the frame reportedly hung empty for the first days because the painter feared the crowd. A joker is said to have looked at the blank space and announced: “There is the deficit!”

When it finally went up, critics praised the velvet and the children but found the queen stiff. The picture did not change anyone's mind. Two years later the Dauphin died too, at seven. Marie Antoinette could no longer walk past the canvas, and had it taken down.
Painter and queen were born in the same year, 1755. Vigée Le Brun painted her about thirty times, and paid for that closeness: she fled France in October 1789 and stayed away for twelve years.

Of the four people in the group, only Marie-Thérèse lived through the Revolution. The queen was guillotined in 1793. The painting survived, and it hangs at Versailles again, in the building it was made for, still making its case to the visitors who file past.

quiz.question: Why was this portrait commissioned?
options: To repair the queen's damaged reputation
As a private gift for the king's bedroom
quiz.explanation: It was ordered in 1785 to present the hated queen as a devoted mother.

quiz.question: What does the large cabinet in the shadows contain?
quiz.explanation: It is a jewel cabinet, pushed into the dark so that the children look like her real treasure.

quiz.question: Who is missing from the cradle?
quiz.explanation: Sophie died in June 1787 before her first birthday.

quiz.question: Which older kind of picture inspired the pyramid shape of the group?
quiz.explanation: The triangle of mother and children comes from Renaissance Madonnas such as Raphael's.

quiz.question: What did Marie Antoinette do with the painting after the Dauphin died in 1789?
options: She gave it to the painter
She had a copy made for Vienna
quiz.explanation: She could no longer bear to walk past it.

facts.text: The queen wears a large diamond necklace in this portrait.
facts.explanation: Her neck is bare, a deliberate choice after the diamond necklace scandal.

facts.text: The painter and Marie Antoinette were born in the same year.
The portrait won back public affection for the queen.
facts.explanation: Critics admired the painting of fabrics and children, but opinion of the queen did not change.
